approach: Teach how Spanish speakers say their names, the everyday titles señor, señora and señorita, and the two-surname system through one worked family, then practice reading names and addressing people.
coverage: Me llamo ... = My name is ...; ¿Cómo te llamas? / ¿Cómo se llama usted?
Pronouncing names: José (hoh-SEH), Juan (hwahn), Jorge (HOR-heh); j is a breathy h
Abbreviations Sr., Sra., Srta. take a capital; written out, the title is lowercase mid-sentence
Two surnames: María García López = first name + first surname + second surname
Traditionally the first surname comes from the father and the second from the mother
People are called by their first surname: la señora García
Women usually keep their own surnames when they marry

blocks.purpose: Introduces names in Spanish and the phrases for giving and asking a name.

paragraphs: To give your name, say Me llamo ... (literally "I call myself"): Me llamo Ana. To ask a friend: ¿Cómo te llamas? To ask someone you address formally: ¿Cómo se llama usted?
Spanish names are said with Spanish sounds. The letter j is a breathy h, so José is hoh-SEH, Juan is hwahn and Jorge is HOR-heh. Names stress where the accent mark says: José, Sofía, Andrés, Lucía.

data.footnote: The short forms take a capital letter (Sr. Ruiz). Written out in the middle of a sentence, the title is lowercase: el señor Ruiz.

blocks.purpose: States the two-surname system as one rule with its parts.

data.anchor: Most Spanish speakers have two surnames: traditionally the first comes from the father and the second from the mother.
prerequisites: María García López: María is her first name, García her first surname, López her second.
She is called by her first surname: la señora García, not la señora López.
Women usually keep their own surnames when they marry.
Some countries now let parents choose which surname goes first.

data.caption: How a child's name is built
rows: Pérez (from her father), then García (from her mother)
data.footnote: Each child takes the first surname of each parent.

blocks.purpose: Applies the system: finding the name used with señora.

data.prompt: A form says: Nombre: Carmen. Apellidos: Torres Medina. How do you address her politely?

feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Read the feedback and try again.

byOption.a: Yes: people are addressed by their first surname.
byOption.b: Medina is her second surname, usually from her mother; it is not the one used with señora.

blocks.purpose: Targets the common mistake of treating the last name written as the "main" surname.

data.question: Your coworker is Luis Ramírez Ortega. Which surname did he most likely get from his father?
data.commonErrorLabel: The last name is not the family name

trapReasons.1: In English the last word of a name is the family name, so Ortega looks like it.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: English puts the family name last, so learners look at the end of a Spanish name.
data.correctReasoning: Traditionally the first surname, Ramírez, comes from the father, and the second, Ortega, from the mother. He is señor Ramírez.
data.recoveryTip: Use the surname right after the first name.

blocks.purpose: Closes with how to give a name and address someone by the right surname.

data.takeaway: Say Me llamo ..., use señor, señora or señorita with the first surname, and remember that García López means García is the name to use.
